idiom_name: duck typing over message presence; a module as the contract (Sorbet interface! / abstract! for static enforcement)
implementation_notes: Ruby has no interface keyword and no anonymous contract type, so the contract is the set of messages an object answers: the classic structure is replaced by naming the required operations in documentation and in a shared conformance test, and by using a Module as the unit of an explicit contract when a nominal name is genuinely needed. A module used as a contract relies on discipline - it can carry shared implementation, so statelessness is a convention, not a rule - and the only language-level marker is NotImplementedError, raised by the stub at call time. Sorbet's abstract!/interface! (via extend T::Helpers) adds enforcement: a module marked interface! may contain only abstract methods with signatures, including classes must implement them, and srb tc rejects violations before the code runs; choose that form when the contract must be checked rather than described.
code_sketch:
# typed: true
module ShapeContract
  extend T::Helpers
  interface!                     # every method must be abstract
  sig { abstract.returns(Float) }
  def area; end
end
class Square
  include ShapeContract          # nominal opt-in; Sorbet checks #area
  def initialize(side) = @side = side
  def area = @side * @side
end
pitfalls: Nothing enforces the contract at definition time: a class that omits a method fails at the call site with NoMethodError, so a shared example group run against every implementation is the usual substitute.
respond_to? checks are shallow - they see the name and arity, not the behaviour - and a method_missing implementation makes them lie in both directions.
Including a module adds its concrete methods and can shadow existing ones (the ancestor chain decides), so giving a contract module a helper method later silently changes every including class.
Sorbet's interface! forbids private and protected members and requires signatures on every method, so internal helpers cannot live in the same module.
